segments.description: Coaches, our next presenter needs very little introduction. We are honoured to have the great Yvonne Lendell join us for our conference. Yvonne was the number one ranked tennis player in the world for an astounding 270 weeks and collected 94 singles titles along the way. He also won eight Grand Slam titles and appeared in a staggering 19 Grand Slam finals throughout his illustrious career. Today he is joined by Wally Massour as they talk through the transition from player to coach. Wally and Yvonne, over to you. Thanks for joining us today and obviously, you know, chatting to you today given your vast experience in tennis as a player and as a coach and a lot of coaches here in Australia are pretty keen to hear some of your insights. But Yvonne, if I could just start. I want to go back to about 1980, 1981. I was a young kid signed by ProServe in Australia. I was heading over to play the US juniors and ProServe actually organised for me to spend four or five days hitting with you and you were very much an established player at the very top of the game. And you did. You hit with me for four or five days in Washington DC with unbelievably hot. And Yvonne, you had this image of quite a hard man, a hard competitor on the court, you were very generous with your time, you were very generous to hit with a young Australian player making his way onto the tour and you continued to be that all through your career as a player,

you know, particularly with the Australians. So I guess what I'm getting at Yvonne is was there a genesis or was there something in you that enjoyed mentoring people or giving of your time? You were always very generous in that regard. Do you think there was something always there for you? Well, Wally, I always enjoyed hitting with younger players. I had, even after that, when I already was doing better on the tour, I had young players to my house and, you know, I had Bill Scanlon, I had Christoban Rensberg, I had Amos Munster, I had Pete Sampras, I had Jared Palmer, I had Lawson Duncan, I had Hendrik Sandström and we would just use it as a training block most of the time. So at times I had even two young players because I needed them to be fresh and that should be meaningful. But it goes back probably to my youth where at our club as a little kid, we had players who would go and practice their serves in the evening, almost still dark, right? And I was seven, eight, nine years old and I was trying to return their serves and pick up the balls and sweep the court. But I was on the court with them, which is always important as you know. And then I will remember forever, I was 16 and I went to Yugoslavia, which today would be known as Slovenia, to a place called Maribor, European Junior Championships. And I won the 16s and under. But one evening I'm kind of wandering around the courts

and there is two guys hitting and they say, hey, Junior, if you have nothing to do, come and hit with us. And we did two on once for two hours every evening and it was Alex Metreveli and Kakulya, two Davis Cabrera Soviet Union players. They were actually from Georgia, a satellite state of Soviet Union. And I saw how great it was for me. And so anytime I could get good practice myself and be with juniors at the same time, it was fantastic. So Ivan, in a sense, you kind of had the benefit of those experiences and that was something that was inculcated in you. So the culture of that, you're from the Eastern Bloc. So the culture in your club, in your country, in the Eastern Bloc, you feel was pretty healthy in that respect, everybody trying to work together to get the best out of themselves. Very, very much so. I was very fortunate to be at that club and I would ball-boy when I was six years old in the club matches and championships and I would be there from 9 a.m. till the last match being done on the courts and ball-boying later on, I would be a lines person and an empire and so on and then I played in it, of course. And every single step, I was always the youngest one for some reason, but I enjoyed that and I knew I'm getting better just by watching. But the culture at our club, well, I'm sorry, I should back up. So from doing that, I could recognize as a young kid already who is talented,

who is not and so on and so on. And we had a couple guys at the club who were not very talented. One of them could not serve. He would serve 15, 17 double folds a match, even underhand double folds and so on. Yet he was there five days a week in the evening trying to serve. And when you're young, you watch that and you look at it and you say, you know, he's trying to get better maybe he's not succeeding as much as he would like to, but if I do the same thing, I am going to get better. And there was another guy, he was a little heavier. Yet every evening for half hour, he would skip rope. So guess what, you get yourself a rope and you go and skip with him too. And things like that form your work ethic, form your character and teach you that hard work can get you somewhere. Ivan, that's a really interesting point you make about your situation as a junior in the club. And I think, you know, with a lot of the coaches listening to this, if you look at the moment, Europe is a real hotbed and Eastern Europe is a real hotbed of producing the very best players in the world, men and women. But I think they have a pretty healthy club scene. And I think we have a few different scenarios in Australia, like in Sydney, for example, a lot of the clubs are owned by councils. And then if a coach wants to work at that particular club, he has to pay a lease. So the moment he finds that lease, you know,

can be up to $15,000 per court, he becomes like a small business operator as opposed to a coach. And the culture is a little bit different. So people come for an hour and play, it's like a piano lesson and then you leave. But what you're talking about is a place that you could spend a lot of time, as you say, jump on and off the court, mix with adults, mix with kids your own age, and enjoy the whole range of experiences that a club can provide. And that for you is pretty healthy. Yes, absolutely. It's very healthy, Wally, as you're saying, but you can go to another club and these guys, they sit down and play cards and have a beer instead of going working. That's why I'm saying I was very fortunate to be around the guys who just go and work. I think you enjoy the world too. Well, you do what you see around yourself. Maybe I would have been a good card player, who knows. But I believe young kids do what they see around themselves. And if they see hard work, they go and work hard. If they see a guy who's serving and volleying, they're going to serve and volley. If they see a guy chipping and charging, they're going to do that. And to set next. And they get formed. Their games and personalities get formed very early. And if they have enough talent and keep working, they have a chance. So, Ivan, I guess another aspect to that is look as a tennis player and then as a coach, you hear a lot of advice.

You get a lot of opinions. You can read it in the media, people around you, family friends. And you've got to have an ability to take advice on board and then figure out what works for you. I mean, do you give yourself some credit for, as you're going up in those few years, particularly in your home club in Czechoslovakia, to give yourself some credit for having the ability to find out what mattered to you and then make it work? Well, I think you have to look again at your surroundings. And I was very fortunate with both parents playing. So we would discuss tennis at home. And they were both accomplished players, especially my mother. And my father was a brilliant tactician on the tennis court. And he played chess on a very high level as well. And you discuss it. You talk about the matches at Borboid. They may have watched or at Borboid for my mother, and I would hear my father telling her after, hey, listen, maybe next time try this, what we taught about did work or didn't work. And I was there on the court feeling it, not just watching it, but feeling it on the court. If you're on that court, you feel it more than if you're in the stands, right? And so I have learned very quickly from young age to differentiate what works, what doesn't, because I'm there on that court, or doing the lines person. And I can see, okay, this guy has been playing young court. And he was coming in on his back and it was getting passed right and left.

That didn't work. So maybe that's not the right way, but he should have tried something else, but that's not his game. So where do you go? And all these variables and more you see it, more you learn, and then you can bisect all the advice you're being given for yourself because somebody will say, well, you shouldn't come into the net on this guy because he passes well, but maybe I'm better than the guy who I just saw doing that and he was getting passed. Maybe my approach is better. Maybe I'm a better baller. And then you start making decisions based on all those things. So Yvonne, you talk about that collegiate sort of atmosphere as you're growing up as a junior, then you get out on the tour. And I guess I'm just trying to deduce what shaped you and what ultimately shaped your coaching philosophy. So you get out on the tour and look, it's pretty cutthroat. Obviously you've got some great rivals, John McEnroe for one. It's pretty tense. You don't have that same atmosphere, I'm assuming where everybody's out to help everybody. You have a few close friends on tour, but it's very much an independent individual sport. So then you start to lean towards your team, your support team and the people in your corner throughout your professional career. So just tell us a little bit about some of those people. And obviously everyone in Australia is very familiar with your relationship with Tony Roach,

but just talk a little bit about some of those mentors and some of the people that you really valued and some of the messages you've got whilst you're a pro. Well, I have to tell you what, even when I was coming up onto the tour, we didn't have support teams. We were all on our own. And I was fortunate again at the time that Czechoslovakia had a lot of players. They probably had eight to 10 players in top 100. So very rarely would you go to a tournament when there was no other Czech player. And unless I went to Asia or to Australia, there were always Czech players and you would hang around and so on and so on. And they took it up in themselves. I will remember one day I have never played, I have never played an ATP tour event. And I was in Florence, Italy, I was 18 years old and I lost last round to qualifying, in qualifying. And I was pretty depressed and I'm having dinner with those guys and the guys are saying, hey, what are you doing tomorrow? I said, I don't know, I don't have any plans. Yes, you do. 9.30, we're on the court, we're practicing. And I was practicing with two guys in top 100, right? And so we took care of each other that way. And just like, you know, I practiced with you and I practiced with young upcoming Czech players at tournaments, so they would come and warm me up and so on. So in some ways we were being used for the better of the better player, but also we were given an incredible opportunity

to practice with better players, right? And then as I got better, I had a first coach which was FIBAQ and he had a lot of experience, he had a lot of experience from Eastern Europe, which was also very helpful how to deal with them. And then in 1984, I was 24 years old, I started being coached from next season by Tony Roach. And that was phenomenal. And I have, I think Tony is one of the best, if not the best coach I have ever seen anywhere. And you know Tony well as well, it might be better than I do. And Tony has a way of delivering the message. He's a hard worker. He is not forceful, but he gets his way when he wants it and so on and so on. And I have really enjoyed working with Tony as a player and then when I became a coach, I have relied quite heavily on what I have learned from those years because when I, Tony and I were together 10 years. And when I sat back after my playing career and thought about it, a lot of things I remembered and a lot of things were applicable to my coaching positions. And I would not hesitate to call him for advice as well. So Ivan, if you consider, I mean there's two great names in tennis that you had in your corner, feedback to start with and obviously Tony. And I think Tony, he loves to work hard. So you were probably a great fit. You were very rigid and very disciplined. And you know Tony likes to work hard and you obviously tried with the hard work.

It's interesting you talk about your father as a great tactician. So now we enter into a phase where you're starting to mentor players. Tony to me was, was he someone that really got involved in opposition and analysis? Or were you more reliant on Tony to prepare you for any eventuality? Well, how did you see his great benefit? Well, one of the reasons I hired Tony was that he was a left-hander. I never practiced with left-handers when I was growing up. We did not have one at our club. So for me playing left-handers was always difficult. And when Tony and I started working together, there were 10 left-handers in top 10. And so that was a difficult time for me, obviously. And so Tony was a master of preparing me for the big occasions. He had an advantage of having to prepare me only for two or three opponents, just like I did when I started coaching Mari. It was just Nova, Grafa and Roger, right? So I could detail every practice for those three guys. I had three different practices. One was a Roger practice, one was a Rafa practice, one was a Nova practice because we needed to work on certain things. He was beating everybody else without me, so I don't need to worry about those things. There is a difference between a player like Andy at that stage or a young player where you need to work on developing skills and you can't work on certain opponents. So that's a huge, huge difference there.

So Tony had an advantage of preparing me against certain players. And he was brilliant at that and telling me what left-handers like and don't like and so on and so on. Okay, well, that's interesting. And I guess I did want to jump to the Mari scenario because Andy and I've always had the utmost respect for Andy as a player. And I kind of felt probably, as you did, that he wasn't maximizing his ability all the time. There were times when he was quite negative on the court. So you talk about your ability through all of your experiences as a player and the mentoring with Tony and the time you spent with some great tennis players and great tennis coaches in the world. But then when I look at Andy, I look at the man management element of it. And I got to admit, I just was wondering how you would cope with some of those scenarios when Andy was under pressure on the court and we know he's quite capable of turning into his box and having a consultation mid-match. But you seem to handle it very stoically. But just talk a little bit about that because obviously you talk about the preparation to the match because then there's the actual man in management leading into the match and during the match. What was your philosophy there? Well, let me start leading into the match. That was very easy. Three of us was Andy, Danny Valverde and myself. And Andy knew exactly how to play everybody and what he wants to do.

So my question would be, what do you think Andy? And he would just lay it out there how he wants to go and play. Then I say, Danny, what do you think? And he would say a couple of things. And then I would say a couple of things if I would either say, hey, that's perfect, just go for it. Or I would say, well, I think this may also work or this may be a good idea. So that was the easy part because Andy was so good at strategy. And I have never seen a player actually who was so good or as good as Andy adjusting mid-match. You don't have to worry with Andy saying, hey, if this is happening, you need to do this. If that is happening, you need to do that. He would figure it out very quickly himself. As far as his outbursts, I knew from my own experience, I knew from ball-boying, I knew from watching other players on the tour that players have to let their anger out and let their emotions out. And if you would put Andy out there and tell him, hey, you know, you just stay passive. You don't say a word. He could not play. And so it's okay with me if the player breaks the racket or fires the ball out of the stadium if he yells at the box as long as it's quick. And then he goes back to, I always say that the time between points is analyze what happened, prepare what you want to happen and catch your breath. So if you take 20 seconds berating yourself and you don't do the RS3, it's a problem.

If you take three seconds berating yourself and start focusing on the RS3, I'm okay with it. Yeah, and there's no doubt that even when he appeared to be losing his mind at times, he was definitely competing. He definitely pulled hard. But Ivan, if you talk about the preparation and obviously talking about the match, let's say you were weeks away, a little bit of a pre-season sort of scenario, how did you take your brand of training and your work ethos and then try to convince Andy who hadn't won a slam at the time, it was being talked about obviously as a player that had the ability to win a slam. Was it tricky to convince him that certain things had to be done in the pre-season that you felt were necessary to take that next step? How did you manage that? No, I believe in a thing called Ape. I call it Ape. Analyze, plan and execute. And training block pre-season is perfect for that. You realize what your players weaknesses are with a young player, what the weaknesses are. Now we have statistics on top of that. So you support it with the statistics. You plan how much you're going to work on everything and then you go and execute it. It's a brainless job. Once you make the plan, it's just brainless. Anybody can do it, right? There are a few elements to that, of course, but if you have a good player already or a great player like Andy, you analyze what he needs to do against those three opponents,

which he's not beating consistently. You plan how you're going to practice it and then you go and execute. But with Andy or anybody else on that level, you also have to sell them on it. So you discuss it and say, you know, this is what I think, what do you think, and we try that. And because of my philosophy, how philosophy of coaching anyone is that we have to have similar philosophies how that person should play. If I'm going to coach you, Wally, and you say, you know, I'm okay serving and bullying, but I think I should stay back more and I'm not going to coach you because I don't believe that's what you should have been doing. And one of us would have to compromise. And then it's no good. Okay, so that's all done before I agree to the job. One, once I agree to the job, I don't have to worry about it because we have kind of discussed it in interviewing each other. And then you just go ahead and do it. Yeah, and even if you, you looked at that experience with Murray and obviously you learn as you go. And as a player, you've got experience, you've got coach's eye. It seems to me you enjoyed the ability to look at data and the technologies was available and you talk about a lot about analyzing things and setting a plan. So I'm kind of assuming that you enjoyed that element of the modern game, the idea that you could break down statistics, look at data, look at vision, and you know, create that plan.

I love numbers. It was my favorite in school, math and physics were my favorite because of the numbers. And once I was at Wimbledon and the prep week and there's not too many people and this scruffy looking guy comes to me and says, hi, I'm such and such with LTA. I said, nice to meet you. And he says, are you interested in statistics for Andy? I go, what do you have in mind? He goes, come with me. I'll show you and took me under the stadium somewhere and showed me and I said, I love it. Absolutely love it. What can I get? How fast can I get it? And so on and so on. And quite interestingly, I had a discussion with somebody else the other day. We all have good eyes. We all have good feel, right? We can see things on the court, but I don't trust my lying eyes all the time. And there was an instant where when he was playing there was a certain pattern and we both agreed he needs to get out of that pattern. So we came up with another pattern. And he beat Djokovic easy in that match using that pattern. And we always talked or I always tried to debrief my player after the match when it's still fresh in his memory. What did you feel? What didn't work? How did you feel about certain shots and so on and so on? And I said, how did you feel about the pattern B? He goes, it was great. I felt so comfortable with it. And it looked good to me too. So I sent a note to the statistician. How did the pattern B work out?

He goes, get away from it. Don't ever do it again. He won one out of three points in it. So even though it looked good to us, it was not very successful. And that's why I say, don't try your lying eyes all the time. So even you talk about that, you know, that ability to look at the data and come up with, you know, meaningful patterns out of the data. But once again, it seems to me that, you know, maybe the art of being a good coach is putting in the work as well. The study, the research, not being too dogmatic, being open minded. So maybe not much different to being a player really, just got to work hard. So what was your first clue that hard work is good? Well, I think it was actually when I hit with you in Washington, D.C. as an 18 year old and I was dying because it was about 35 degrees and 95 percent humidity and you were barely breathing. I thought I've got a bit of work to do. So yeah, it seems to me that hard work might be important. Yeah. No, it's that's what I, we all know that and with Andy and even if it's very hard, he worked hard as well. It's, it's easy to work with players who want to work. I don't have it in me to motivate player to work. I need a motivated player so I can do my job. I'm much better at coming up with the patterns, coming up with the practices than motivating the player to work hard. Ivan, we, we, we could go on quite a while here, but I'll just ask you another question on there.

So I'm assuming I coached a little bit, you know, after the tour and I coached some professional players. I spent some time with Michael Stick and I made a mistake with Michael Stick because I tried to solve his problems through my eyes. I was too inexperienced to realize I needed to step aside and I needed to understand what he was feeling and try to solve the problem through his eyes. So you work with someone like Andy Murray, great player, you win Grand Slans, you now move on to one of the next big things with Zverev. How did you find out, you know, in the sense that you, you probably had come to some conclusions with Andy that this worked. Now all of a sudden you've got a different athlete, a different player, different mindset. How did you cope with that transition? Well, as I said earlier, you have a top player which is made and you just use what he has. And then you have a young player which is still forming and it's your job to try to form him into a better player. So for example, the second serve, everybody always talked about second serve. We worked quite hard and or there were other instances and I don't like to name things because they are still playing, right? But there were other things which he needed to improve. And then you just set on two, three-year process. If you lasted long, most of the times you don't, but if you lasted long, two, three-year process to make him a better player

and then you start worrying more about the patterns. You can't do it all at once, it just doesn't happen. I like to, I like to, whether it's with juniors or whether it is with the top pros, I like to focus on two, two, three things max and then reevaluate three months later where I can take some time away from it and go on to something else. You look at certain weaknesses and I could name them, but again, I prefer not to. And I never touched them because they were coming up once or twice a match and he still did okay and I would have to spend 20 minutes a day on it. I prefer to spend the 20 minutes somewhere else. Okay, so Ivan, imagine we're on a Zoom call here, but imagine you're in a room, you're surrounded by coaches here in Australia and you kind of touched on it with the guy at your club that was serving and he wasn't necessarily getting better. But we can respect that journey, Calhoy, and we understand that coaches, some coaches in the coach, brilliant players, some coaches in the coach, some very motivated players that aren't going to go anywhere, but they're still enjoyable to coach that person. So you're standing in a room with all these coaches, Ivan. Give me three things. What are three things that you would say to them on their coaching, mentoring journey? Because let's face it too, when you coach a player, you have a bit of input into their life too, don't you? You're dealing with them as a person as well.

So just off the top of your head, give me three things that you think would resonate. Well, number one, I would say you cannot ask anything more than that person trying every practice and every match. Win or lose, that's a success, right? Because as you're saying later in life, it's going to come and help them, no matter what they do, whether they go into coaching themselves or whether they go into business, if they're hard workers, they're going to do well. The one thing I would say to the coaches is you really have to know your player. And I know many of these coaches probably coach more than one player, more than one kid. And you really have to know them. Each one of them is different. We did not speak about my time with the USDA. I had a group of six, 15 and 16 year olds. And if you came on the three courts we're practicing, you would never see the three courts doing the same thing because they all have different needs. If your service is good and we're all going to serve, I'm not really doing you volley any favor, right? I'm kind of trading water for you, but you need to return because your return is not so good. Well, I have you returning on one of the courts. So I'm really improving you as well. So that's important. And as I said, you really have to know your player because even in the pros, if we're working on something and I need to get enough repetitions on that, there are a few scenarios.

Number one, you're terrible at it. And I can stay with it for a while because you're a good player, you're going to get better. But I may so destroy you mentally that it's not worth it. Another scenario, you're fantastic at it. But I still have to get away from it pretty quickly because you're only going to get worse and start missing. And if I stay there too long, I'm going to destroy the benefit I just gave you with your confidence. So what I will do, I will do some other drill. And then after another successful drill, I will come back to it when you're in good frame of mind because you just did something well and try to do it again and hoping that you do well and I get enough reps. And you have to know your player. And I can't say it enough because each player reacts differently to it. And you have to know when they're just getting annoyed and so on. I learned very quickly from Danny Valverde. We're practicing at Kibis Cain one year. And he comes to me after about 50 minutes, he goes, you have about five more minutes. I look around, there is no the cloud in the sky. I go, what are you talking about? He's gone. He's losing it. He will be gone in five minutes. I'm thinking, what are you talking about, right? About 10 minutes later, total meltdown. So I learned very quickly to listen to people who know them well. So one day we come there and then he goes, it's going to be a really bad practice today. I go, why?

He's in terrible mood and he's tired. So I looked at Jess Green, who was his conditioning guy. I said, what did you do yesterday? He says, we did a lot of heavy weights. He is tired. So I talked to Andy. I say, Andy, you know what? You did a lot of work yesterday and this and that. And why don't instead of Friday, why don't we take tomorrow off? And I will see you Friday. He goes, okay, I suggest do something nicer. And I told the physio to make good stretch and give him a massage. And we had great practice on Friday or whatever day it was, right? So you have to know your player. And I learned to listen to Danny because he knew him really well. So if I could say, if there's a coach in clubland, they've probably got to have a two or three year plan, as you spoke about, to where they want to take that player to the next level, hopefully. But within that two to three year plan, they've got to be pretty fluid and they've got to really understand the situation that they're in and make a call, not necessarily on a daily basis, but really understand the situation and know where the personality of that player meets their ability to drive them and push them. So look, I really think that's a great message. And Ivan, as I said, we probably could talk a little longer about tennis. You've got so much experience and I really do appreciate your time. I have time. It's only whatever, six, thirty, seven o'clock. I don't go to bed till eight.

Yeah, I just think the, yeah, they're packaging this up to the conference. Yeah, Ivan, look, I do want to thank you for your time. And I want to thank you. Sorry to interrupt before you do that. One thing I'm going to say to the coaches on the club level. One thing which is really important is technique. I have also ran an academy in Hilton Head, and we spent a lot of time fixing bad technique at 14 and 15. Those are years when these players, young kids, need to learn how to compete already. And it's very difficult to change things. Then we got two kids from a junior program which came to us. They were 11 or 12. And their technique was really, really good. And I kind of inquired, how did that happen? And they had this PV program where they played with those orangey balls and smaller called the soft balls which don't bounce. And they don't have to hit the balls on the fence above their head and they have to hit through the ball and all that. And I was kind of skeptical about it. And I became a big fan of that system. I can't remember the name of it, whatever you call it, right? But you know what I'm talking about. And those two kids started improving very quickly because we didn't have to fix anything and we could just let them grow and get stronger physically and learn how to play the game. There is a difference in my opinion between teacher and a coach in both golf and tennis.

And teacher is the one who teaches, teaches Mrs. Smith and Mrs. Jones, and teaches young kids their fundamentals. Coaches are the ones who teach you how to play the game. And that's a, in my opinion, that's a huge difference. But fundamentals and we didn't touch on that. I was extremely, extremely lucky that as a kid, we had a great teacher over there at our home club who was working only with the kids. It was a little different system. You would go, he would, you would go to him and he would start teaching you fundamentals. Then you would move up to another coach. It was not that the coach was moving with you all the time like it's in America and possibly in Australia. And they would give you to another coach and then eventually you would have 100% technique, 200% match play. And in between you would go 80% technique, 60, 40, 20. So it would be on a scale like that where you were less technique all the time and more strategy and match play later on. And the kids who had good technique and were able to do it were the ones who improved the most. That is a great point and it was remiss of me not to bring that up because I think for some of the coaches on this call, that would really resonate because we talk about the club situation in Australia and the financial constraints that they have to run their business. And I might actually conclude them from spending the time that they might like with some of their junior players to establish that technique.

And Yvonne, if I could make an observation in Australia because I worked at Home Bush for Kenneth Australia and we would get kids. James Duckworth, Jordan Thompson, Alex Diminar was here and various players. And it was kind of interesting because sometimes we would get very small young kids with very extreme grips. And it was always a little bit confusing to me because they weren't necessarily strong enough to take advantage of those extreme grips. They would have been far better off with more neutral grips and more linear swing.
